and intelligible and we would be able to go on our way with
glad and grateful hearts. But which of us is there for whom
the world and destiny do not again and again grow dark,
sinister and puzzling? Who is there who has ceased to ask:
why? Who has ceased to lament over the burden of pain and
sorrow, disillusionment and shattered hopes? Which of us
has no fear of fate and death? And further: which of us can be
satisfied with himself so that his whole being is irradiated by
sunny contentment? Who is not tortured by the problems of
his own life, by his weakness and inadequacy, by his guilt?
Who must not confess that listlessness and irritation, dark
passions, untruthfulness, cowardice, or impurity, again and
again overcome him? Which of us therefore could always con-
fess with a grateful heart: "I believe that God has created me"?
But if we honestly confess all this, we also know what
miracle essentially must mean: namely, such a happening as
makes us profoundly aware that in spite of everything, in
spite of all the mysteries of the world and of our destiny, in
spite of the torment of our self-condemnation, God has
created us by His grace, and holds us in His Creator's hand.
And just then, and only then, when we focus our attention
on this one great marvel, can we be aware of the miraculous
in our experience. For when we are moved by this central
question, the Word of Jesus comes home to us.
III
Our story tells us that Jesus invites the disciples to catch
fish after they have toiled all the night and taken nothing.
Left to themselves, they would have abandoned their efforts.
And just then comes the extraordinary command: "Put out
into the deep and let down your nets for a catch!"-into
the deep, i.e. where a catch of fish is most improbable. The
story teaches us that the wonder-working word of Jesus comes
to us precisely when our own resources are exhausted. Weshall
